strengths: The proposed spanning-tree traversal is a simple, original, and intuitively motivated way to retain spatial locality while exposing a causal autoregressive model to diverse generation orders. It requires only next-position embeddings rather than a specialized generator architecture.

The work addresses a meaningful limitation of raster-order visual autoregressive models: conditioning on spatially irregular observations. The BFS-based construction and rejection-sampling algorithm provide a concrete mechanism for turning connected-region inpainting into postfix completion.

The empirical study is substantial in scale. STAR is evaluated from 261M to 1.5B parameters on ImageNet-1k, consistently improves substantially over RandAR in FID, and remains competitive with strong raster-order models while obtaining higher Inception Scores at several scales.

The ablations are informative: Table 2 separates training and inference orders, while Table 3 evaluates BFS versus DFS and shows that BFS normally finds an admissible completion order in fewer than five trials with no reported failures.
The paper is generally clear and provides useful implementation details, hyperparameters, pseudocode, and qualitative samples, making the central method reasonably reproducible.
weaknesses: The evidence for the central image-editing benefit is not fully convincing. The main comparison uses RAR, whose order anneals toward raster scan and is structurally ill-suited to arbitrary masks. Stronger and more relevant baselines such as RandAR, permutation-trained causal models at matched scales, masked-token generators, and established inpainting methods are absent from the main inpainting evaluation.

The inpainting metrics are unconditional whole-image FID and IS. Because the visible portion is copied from a real validation image, these measures can improve without the generated region being conditionally correct, perceptually coherent, or faithful at the boundary. Mask-region perceptual metrics, human evaluation, and more extensive side-by-side examples are needed.

The ablation weakens the claimed editing advantage of spanning-tree training: random-order training followed by spanning-tree inference obtains inpainting FID 2.43, close to STAR's 2.39, and slightly better IS. No uncertainty estimates or repeated runs establish that this difference is meaningful.

STAR does not preserve raster-order generation quality completely: its FID is worse than matched-size RAR at every scale in Table 1. Claims of maintaining sampling performance should therefore be qualified as a trade-off, especially because guidance settings vary by model and no likelihood evaluation is reported.

Claims of unchanged training complexity are unsupported by runtime or throughput measurements; sampling a uniform spanning tree per sequence may impose nontrivial CPU and input-pipeline overhead. Inference rejection-sampling time is likewise reported only as trial counts, not latency.

The method assumes connected masked and unmasked regions and at least one visible corner. This excludes common editing patterns such as multiple disjoint holes, arbitrary known pixels, and masks covering all corners; these limitations and possible extensions are not discussed experimentally.

The entropy analysis is suggestive rather than causal: it reports model predictive entropy without showing that center bias or entropy uniformity explains the generation gains. The formal objectives also maximize probabilities rather than expected log-likelihood despite the stated maximum-likelihood training, which should be corrected.

strengths: The paper presents a clear and reasonably original Algorithms/General contribution: using breadth-first traversals of uniform spanning trees to obtain structured yet variable autoregressive generation orders.
STAR is simple to integrate into a causal decoder-only Transformer, requiring mainly next-position conditioning rather than a specialized image-generation architecture.

The ImageNet-1k study is substantial, covering four model sizes up to 1.5B parameters. STAR consistently improves over the random-order RandAR models and approaches strong raster-scan RAR performance.

The ablations usefully separate training and inference orders, and the comparison of BFS and DFS provides empirical support for the proposed completion procedure. Implementation hyperparameters and mask-generation pseudocode are also supplied.
The manuscript is generally organized well, and its diagrams communicate the central construction effectively.
weaknesses: The central image-editing claim is inadequately validated. Inpainting is compared only with RAR, omitting particularly relevant arbitrary-order, masked-token, diffusion, and dedicated inpainting baselines. This makes it unclear whether spanning-tree ordering is competitive beyond the selected baseline.

The evaluation covers only synthetic connected masks for which both masked and observed regions remain connected and at least one corner is visible. These assumptions exclude disconnected holes, multiple edited regions, contexts split by a mask, and other common editing configurations; the paper neither evaluates nor emphasizes this restricted applicability.

FID and Inception Score of completed images provide weak evidence of conditional editing quality because they do not measure consistency with the observed context, agreement with the intended completion, boundary artifacts, or perceptual plausibility. Figure 7 contains very few examples and does not clearly visualize masks or boundaries. No human evaluation or conditional reconstruction metric is reported.

Unconditional generation remains consistently worse in FID than the matched-size RAR models: 2.24 versus 1.95 at B and 1.55 versus 1.48 at XXL. Thus the claimed preservation of sampling performance is approximate and involves a measurable trade-off.

The justification based on sample-space size is incomplete: many spanning trees can induce the same BFS order, and uniformly sampling trees does not uniformly sample traversal orders. Comparing the number of trees with N! therefore does not establish that the resulting order distribution is intrinsically better. The proposed center-bias explanation is mostly conjectural rather than causally demonstrated.

The likelihood presentation is mathematically imprecise. Equations 2 and 4 optimize an expectation of products, whereas sampled cross-entropy training corresponds to an expectation of log-likelihoods; order-dependent conditionals also need not define a single consistent joint distribution.

There are no repeated-run uncertainties or significance estimates, and computational costs are not reported despite training four models for roughly 400 epochs. Rejection-sampling overhead is tested only on the 16-by-16 token lattice, leaving behavior at higher resolutions unestablished.

Reproducibility is weakened by the empty code link ('The code is available at .'). Important details such as evaluation sample counts and a fully specified comparison protocol for RAR inpainting are also insufficiently explicit.

Overall, the method is promising, but the evidence does not yet convincingly support the broad image-editing and performance-preservation claims. The balance therefore slightly favors rejection rather than a strong rejection.

strengths: Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution, STAR offers a simple and original structured alternative to random token permutations: breadth-first traversal of uniform spanning trees preserves local connectivity while allowing substantially more ordering flexibility than raster scan.

The method is technically intuitive and integrates into a standard causal decoder-only Transformer with only next-position embeddings, making it potentially useful for existing autoregressive image generators and future multimodal models.

The empirical results are strong. Across four model scales on ImageNet-1k, STAR substantially outperforms the directly relevant RandAR models and approaches raster-order RAR performance; STAR-XXL obtains 1.55 FID and 338.8 IS while retaining inpainting functionality.

The controlled STAR-B ablations isolate the effect of the ordering strategy: spanning-tree training improves generation markedly over random permutations and improves inpainting over raster scan. The DFS/BFS experiment also supports the proposed traversal and root-selection choices.

The paper is clearly organized, visually polished, and reasonably reproducible from the supplied algorithm, architectural configurations, training hyperparameters, masking procedure, and sampling settings.
weaknesses: The inpainting evidence is narrower than the claims suggest. Evaluation uses only synthetic connected masks that leave at least one corner unmasked and keep the unmasked region connected; STAR therefore does not support arbitrary disconnected observations or masks covering every corner. The claimed flexibility should be qualified accordingly.

Editing comparisons are insufficient. The main comparison is against raster-order RAR, which is structurally unable to condition naturally on arbitrary observed regions, while direct editing-capable competitors such as RandAR, MaskGIT-style models, or diffusion inpainting methods are absent. Table 2 includes a random-order baseline only at the smallest scale.

Whole-image FID and IS are incomplete measures of conditional inpainting because observed pixels can dominate the score and these metrics do not assess fidelity inside the mask, boundary consistency, or compatibility with the context. Mask-region perceptual metrics, human evaluation, and more qualitative examples would strengthen the editing claim.

The assertion that STAR adds no meaningful complexity is not fully substantiated. Wilson sampling and inference-time rejection introduce overhead, yet only trial counts—not wall-clock latency, throughput, or preprocessing cost—are reported.

Some explanatory arguments remain conjectural: the connection between uniform conditional entropy and generation quality is correlational, and reducing the combinatorial order space does not by itself establish why the selected distribution is optimal. Equations 1–2 also use products inside maximization/expectation where an expected log-likelihood formulation would be more precise.

Results lack repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, and sensitivity analyses for tree sampling, tie-breaking, and guidance settings. The manuscript also displays an empty code URL, weakening the otherwise good reproducibility case.

strengths: Under the default Algorithms/General contribution type, STAR is a simple and original way to reconcile flexible autoregressive ordering with image locality: BFS traversals of corner-rooted uniform spanning trees give connected-prefix orders while retaining an essentially standard decoder-only Transformer.

The method is technically motivated and accompanied by a constructive postfix-completion algorithm. The rejection-sampling study over 50k masks supports the choice of BFS over DFS, with fewer than five trials on average and no reported failures for the evaluated masks.

The empirical study is substantial in scale. Four ImageNet-1k models from 261M to 1.5B parameters are evaluated, and matched-budget ablations compare raster scan, random permutation, annealed orders, and spanning-tree orders. STAR consistently improves substantially over unrestricted permutation and outperforms similarly sized RandAR models.

The paper provides both generation and inpainting results, analyses of locality, center bias, conditional entropy, sampling overhead, and a supplementary representation-learning experiment. Hyperparameters and compute costs are reported in useful detail.
Presentation is generally clear, and the manuscript explicitly identifies the restrictions on admissible masks rather than concealing them.
weaknesses: The central claim that flexibility is obtained without sacrificing generation performance is overstated. In the controlled Table 3 comparison, STAR is worse than raster scan in FID (2.24 versus 2.04) and recall (0.57 versus 0.59), though better in IS and precision. At matched scales in Table 1, STAR also has consistently worse FID than RAR. The result is therefore a useful trade-off rather than unequivocal preservation of sampling quality.

The inpainting evidence is not sufficiently comprehensive for the main editing claim. Evaluation uses a custom connected random-mask distribution that explicitly excludes masks covering all corners or disconnecting the observed region, exactly the cases STAR cannot handle in one pass. Results are averaged over masking ratios, obscuring behavior by mask size, and only two qualitative comparisons are shown. Standard free-form, box, outpainting, and disconnected-mask settings would make the case much stronger.

FID, IS, precision, and recall on whole completed images mainly measure output distribution quality and are influenced by the unchanged ground-truth region. They do not directly quantify boundary coherence, consistency with the observed context, or reconstruction behavior in the edited region. Mask-region perceptual measures and a human preference or compatibility study are missing.

The proposed multi-turn remedy for unsupported masks is only illustrated conceptually; it is neither specified as a complete algorithm nor evaluated for quality, accumulated errors, or runtime. Moreover, the rejection experiment covers single connected masks, leaving efficiency for multiple mask components insufficiently supported.

The ablations establish the benefit over unrestricted permutation but do not isolate whether uniform spanning trees are important relative to simpler locality-preserving alternatives, such as randomized connected-frontier growth or randomized grid BFS. Since the Transformer receives the order rather than the tree itself, this comparison is important to substantiate the specific algorithmic contribution.

Several analyses remain correlational or underspecified: the center-bias quartiles lack enough construction detail, the entropy results motivate but do not establish the claimed convergence mechanism, and no multiple-seed variability or confidence intervals are reported despite relatively modest differences among some large-model results. The manuscript's displayed code-availability statement also contains no usable link, limiting current reproducibility.

strengths: The paper presents an original and intuitive Algorithms/General contribution: BFS traversal of uniformly sampled spanning trees provides a structured family of autoregressive orders that preserves locality while allowing many conditioning orders. The rejection-sampling construction for postfix completion is technically interesting and requires only modest architectural modification.

The experimental scale is substantial: four model sizes up to 1.5B parameters are trained on ImageNet-1k, with generation results competitive with strong autoregressive baselines. STAR consistently improves over RandAR in the reported generation metrics and scales predictably.

Table 3 provides a useful controlled comparison under the STAR-B compute budget. It supports the central claim that spanning-tree orders offer a better generation/inpainting trade-off than unrestricted random permutations or permutation-to-tree annealing.

The paper includes relevant analyses of locality, root selection, conditional entropy, traversal strategy, rejection-sampling efficiency, and computational overhead. In particular, the DFS-versus-BFS experiment directly supports an important design choice.

The method is clearly motivated and mostly well explained. Hyperparameters, training costs, masking construction, and key implementation choices are documented, and the paper explicitly discusses masks that violate its assumptions.
weaknesses: The inpainting evidence does not adequately establish conditional completion quality. FID, IS, precision, and recall are computed on whole images that retain real unmasked content; these distribution-level metrics can be strongly influenced by the observed region and do not measure whether the generated region is coherent with its particular context. There is no masked-region evaluation, boundary-consistency measure, perceptual or semantic correspondence test, or human study.

The inpainting benchmark is tailored to the method's feasibility conditions: masks are generated until the remaining lattice is connected and at least one corner remains visible. Realistic masks that cover all corners, separate the observations, contain complex shapes, or require multiple turns are excluded. The proposed multi-turn remedy is supported only by one qualitative example, so the broad image-editing and arbitrary-region claims are overstated.

Comparisons among inpainting methods are not well controlled. STAR and RandAR receive observations as prefixes, RAR uses teacher forcing, and DiT uses latent blending; implementation quality and tuning for these substantially different procedures are unclear. Averaging metrics over masking ratios from 0.1 to 0.9 further conceals important regime-specific behavior.

The claim that STAR preserves generation performance is only partially supported. In the controlled Table 3 experiment, raster scan has better FID than STAR (2.04 versus 2.24), and matched RAR models have consistently better FID in Table 1. STAR improves IS and gains editing flexibility, but the paper does not quantify uncertainty or report multiple training seeds, making small differences difficult to interpret.

The formal objective is imprecise. Equations 2 and 4 describe maximizing an expectation of likelihood products, whereas the stated cross-entropy training corresponds to maximizing expected log likelihood. These are different objectives by Jensen's inequality. The paper also provides empirical observations rather than a formal justification that its restricted order family gives the claimed modeling advantages.

The empirical scope is narrow relative to the claimed general building-block status: generation and editing are demonstrated only for class-conditional 256x256 ImageNet images with one VQ tokenizer. There are no higher-resolution, text-conditioned, out-of-domain, or early-fusion multimodal experiments, and the center-bias analysis lacks a convincing definition, uncertainty estimates, and validation beyond ImageNet.

Qualitative inpainting evidence is sparse and difficult to assess: Figure 6 shows only two examples and does not clearly visualize the masks or boundaries. Failure cases, samples under difficult mask configurations, and comparisons across several random completions are absent. The manuscript also states that code is available but supplies no actual repository link, weakening reproducibility.

strengths: The paper introduces an original and well-motivated sequence-order family for autoregressive image generation. BFS traversals of lattice spanning trees preserve locality and a corner-to-center bias while retaining enough order flexibility for postfix completion; this is a meaningful algorithmic contribution rather than merely an architectural modification.

The empirical results support the central generation-quality claim. On ImageNet-1k at 256×256, STAR consistently outperforms the comparable random-order RandAR models and approaches the strong raster-scan RAR baseline, with STAR-XXL obtaining FID 1.55 and IS 338.8. The fixed-budget ablation in Table 3 provides particularly useful evidence that the gain comes from the structured order rather than simply changing the inference order.

STAR offers a compelling generation/inpainting trade-off. STAR-L and STAR-XL substantially improve the reported inpainting FID over DiT, RAR, and RandAR while retaining competitive unconditional generation, and the qualitative examples show better coherence with visible context.

The method is technically simple and incurs little reported overhead. Algorithm 1 explains how BFS and rejection sampling support postfix completion, while the 50k-mask study demonstrates fewer than five trials on average and no failures for the tested connected masks.

The paper is generally clear and includes useful analyses of locality, center bias, conditional entropy, traversal strategy, scaling, and representation learning. Detailed architecture, optimization, sampling, compute, and masking configurations improve reproducibility.
weaknesses: The inpainting evaluation is not fully conclusive. Competing methods use materially different conditioning procedures—prefix completion for STAR/RandAR, teacher forcing for RAR, and latent blending for DiT—and whole-image FID/IS can be dominated by unchanged observed pixels, especially at low masking ratios. Results separated by masking ratio are only shown for RAR versus STAR, and comparisons with specialized inpainting systems, localized masked-region metrics, perceptual studies, or more extensive qualitative examples are absent.

Single-turn postfix completion assumes that the mask leaves at least one corner unmasked and that the observed region remains connected. These restrictions exclude realistic masks. The proposed multi-turn workaround is illustrated but not quantitatively evaluated, so claims of native support for arbitrary region-level editing should be narrowed.

The experimental scope is limited to class-conditional ImageNet generation at 256×256 with one VQ tokenizer and closely related transformer configurations. Results on higher resolutions, text conditioning, other datasets, or data with weaker center bias would better establish generality, particularly because center bias is part of the motivation.

At inference, the tree is constructed conditionally using a farthest-corner root and separate trees for observed and masked regions, whereas training samples uniform spanning trees from random corners. The paper does not isolate the effect of this distribution shift or compare alternative conditioned-tree samplers; efficiency is also evaluated only on the paper's synthetic connected-mask distribution.

Some formal and reproducibility details need correction. Equations 2 and 4 write an expectation of likelihood products rather than the expected log-likelihood apparently optimized with cross-entropy, uncertainty or repeated-run variation is generally unreported, and the manuscript's code-availability statement contains no accessible URL. Reproducing the largest experiments is additionally costly, reaching 385 A100-GPU days.
